data_description.device_key: 10-character hex key unique to your device (e.g. bd236b1695). You can override it here if needed.
data_description.continuous_connection: Keep the Bluetooth connection open permanently instead of polling every 30 seconds. Captures infrequent sensor updates (e.g. battery voltage) but blocks the official app from connecting at the same time.
data_description.poll_interval: How often (in seconds) to connect and pull sensor data when not using continuous mode. Range: 10–600. Default: 30.
data_description.stale_timeout: How long (in minutes) to keep showing the last known values after a failed poll before marking entities as unavailable. Range: 1–120. Default: 15.
data_description.runtime_max_minutes: Maximum plausible runtime value in minutes. When firmware reports a value above this (e.g. during charging or idle), the sensor is clamped to this value instead of going Unknown. Default: 5940 (99 h). Increase if you have a large device stack capable of genuine runtimes over 99 h.
data_description.debug_attr_logging: Log parsed attribute values with packet classification to a CSV in your HA config folder. Includes direction (TX/RX), command type (cmd1/cmd2_resp/cmd3_resp), packet index, and parsed values.
data_description.debug_raw_logging: Log every raw BLE packet (TX and RX) with direction and command classification to a CSV in your HA config folder. Useful for diagnosing missing settings responses.
data_description.open_id: Only for stations that advertise the BLE name WP - the Guardian / D5 V2 family, e.g. the Guardian 6000 V2. Enter the openId of the Cleanergy/OUPES account that owns the station (it is in the cloud device record). Leave empty for TT stations such as the Mega 1.
data_description.user_id: Numeric user id of the same Cleanergy/OUPES account, returned by the cloud login. Required together with the openId on WP stations; leave at 0 for TT stations. Changing either value re-pairs the station.
data_description.cloud_email: Fill both cloud fields to have openId and userId read from the vendor cloud for you. Used for that single request only: the options this dialog writes are built field by field, and the cloud fields are not among them, so they cannot land in Home Assistant's .storage or in a backup. Home Assistant's own debug logging may still echo form input — if that matters to you, leave these blank and fill in openId and userId above instead. Either route ends up identical.
data_description.cloud_password: Sent over plain HTTP (the vendor offers no HTTPS endpoint) and discarded after the request. Nothing in this integration retains it.

init.description:
Your Cleanergy email and password are **not saved anywhere.** They are sent to the vendor once, to look up openId and userId, and then dropped — this integration stores only the values it reads back. Omit them and nothing changes except that you type those two values yourself.

Note that the vendor API is plain HTTP with no HTTPS endpoint, so the credentials cross the network unencrypted, exactly as they do in the official app.

The identity stored here was {identity_source}.

account_number.title: Your Cleanergy User ID
account_number.description:
Enter the Cleanergy user ID that **{name}** was paired with, and Home Assistant derives the binding key from it.

The Cleanergy app does not display this number anywhere, so do not spend the evening looking for a screen. If this entry was set up with the cloud sign-in, Home Assistant already fetched the value and you will not need this screen; an existing entry that used that sign-in shows it under Configure on the OUPES card. An entry built from a hand-entered device key has never learned it.

The station was written with that number and a key generated from it when the app paired it, so this is the only value needed - no device key to capture, and no cloud lookup. You can leave the app installed but closed: the station answers one Bluetooth client at a time, and Home Assistant keeps that connection open continuously. Removing the station from the app would wipe the pairing and is not needed here.

error.cloud_identity_login_failed: Sign-in to the Cleanergy cloud failed. Check the email and password, or go back and choose a different method. Credentials are used once and never stored.
error.cloud_identity_no_open_id: Signed in and found the station, but the vendor's records for it did not include the numeric user ID that the Bluetooth key is derived from. The Home Assistant log names the fields that were present, so you can tell an account without one from a vendor that renamed the field. If you know the number, type it in above; if not, switch back and enter a device key you already have.
error.cloud_identity_no_user_id: Signed in and found the station, but the numeric account id (userId) could not be read from the response. Try again; if it keeps happening, enter openId and userId yourself instead.
error.cloud_identity_not_bound: This station is not in that account's device list. Add it in the Cleanergy app first — a Guardian / D5 V2 only carries the account identity after the app has bound it — then try again.
error.invalid_device_key: Device key must be exactly 10 hexadecimal characters (e.g. bd236b1695).
error.invalid_open_id: openId must be 32 ASCII characters or fewer - that is all the station's AUTH frame can carry.
error.invalid_user_id: That is not a usable user ID. It is the numeric id of the Cleanergy account the station was paired with, and it is not shown anywhere in the Cleanergy app. An existing entry in Home Assistant reports it - open the cog on the OUPES card, then Configure - and a vendor password login returns it as `uid`.

Setting up **{name}** ({address}).

Choose how you want to provide the device key needed for BLE communication.

create_key.title: Create New Device Key
create_key.description:
This will pair **{name}** ({address}) with a new device key over Bluetooth.

**Before clicking Submit:**
1. Press and hold the **IoT button** on the device for **5 seconds**
2. Wait until the indicator light **flashes rapidly** (factory reset complete)
3. The IoT module (Wi-Fi/BLE) will turn off — **press the IoT button once to turn it back on**
4. The device is now in pairing mode


**One more thing before Submit:** close the Cleanergy app and switch the phone's Bluetooth off. The station serves a single Bluetooth client, so an app still holding it fails this step in a way that looks like a broken integration. And once pairing succeeds the app stops reporting this station until you re-add it - Home Assistant has just written a different key over the one the app stored.
A random key has been generated below. You can change it or leave the default. Pairing takes about 20 seconds.

**WiFi credentials:** these are only used to hand your network to the device so the **vendor app and cloud** can reach it. Home Assistant talks to the device over Bluetooth either way, so leaving both fields blank is the normal choice - and Guardian / D5 V2 devices do not accept them at all.

existing_key.title: Enter Existing Device Key
existing_key.description:
Enter the 10-character hex device key for **{name}** ({address}).

You can find this key by:
- Running `adb logcat | findstr 8888888888888888888` while opening the Cleanergy app
- Checking a btsnoop/PCAPdroid capture of the Cleanergy app traffic
- Using the Cleanergy cloud API via the PowerShell script in the README

cloud_login.description:
Log in with your Cleanergy app credentials to automatically fetch the device key for **{name}** ({address}).

Your credentials are used **once** to retrieve the key and are **not stored**.

⚠️ The Cleanergy API uses unencrypted HTTP — this mirrors the official app's own behaviour.

reconfigure.title: Re-pair / Reconfigure Device
reconfigure.description:
Re-pair **{name}** ({address}) without removing it from Home Assistant — all entity IDs and history are kept.

**Just re-sending credentials?** Leave *Re-run BLE pairing* unchecked and fill in your WiFi details: the stored device key and credentials are pushed over Bluetooth without a factory reset. Guardian / D5 V2 devices cannot take WiFi credentials this way, so on those, tick *Re-run BLE pairing* instead.

**Full re-pair?** Tick *Re-run BLE pairing* and put the device into pairing mode first:
1. Press and hold the **IoT button** for **5 seconds**
2. Wait until the indicator light **flashes rapidly** (factory reset complete)
3. The IoT module (Wi-Fi/BLE) will turn off — **press the IoT button once to turn it back on**

The device is re-claimed with the key below, so it stays the same device to Home Assistant.

data_description.name: Shown in Home Assistant. Changing it does not rename existing entities.
data_description.address: Example: 8C:D0:B2:A7:EC:AF. Only change this if the device's Bluetooth address actually changed.
data_description.device_key: The existing 10-character hex key is pre-filled. Keep it to re-pair as the same device; change it only if you want to program a new key.
data_description.rerun_pairing: Runs the full claim sequence (about 20 seconds). The device must be in pairing mode. Leave unchecked to only re-send credentials.
data_description.wifi_ssid: Only used to hand your network to the station so the **vendor app and cloud** can reach it. Home Assistant keeps using Bluetooth afterwards, so leaving this blank costs you nothing. **Not available on Guardian / D5 V2 stations.**
data_description.wifi_psk: Password for the network named above. Same caveat: it configures the station's own connection for the vendor app, not the connection Home Assistant uses.

identity.title: Account identity
identity.description: The {name} family (Guardian / D5 V2) puts your account identity inside the Bluetooth authentication frame, so the station cannot be used without it. Home Assistant could not recover it from your OUPES / Cleanergy cloud account, usually because the station is not currently added to that account. Easiest fix: go back, add the station in the Cleanergy app first, and fetch it automatically. Otherwise enter the two values below, read from the device record of the account the station belongs to.

data.open_id: Open ID (optional, not checked by the station)

data_description.open_id: The station's openId as stored in its cloud device record - up to 32 characters. It is not the Bluetooth pairing code and not the device key.
data_description.user_id: The numeric account id the station belongs to (0 for a Mega station).

local_claim.title: Claim without a cloud account
local_claim.description:
{name} will be claimed with an identity generated here on your machine: a device key, an openId and an account id, all written into the station over Bluetooth. Nothing is sent to OUPES / Cleanergy, no account or password is needed, and the station works with no internet at all.

This only works on a **factory-reset** station - hold the IoT button for 5 seconds until it flashes rapidly. A station still bound to an app rejects it, because it already stores someone else's identity; use the Cleanergy cloud method for those.

Before you continue, understand what this costs: these values exist only in Home Assistant and cannot be looked up in the vendor cloud, and if the official app binds this station later it overwrites them. Undoing it means factory-resetting the station and adding it in the app.

data.confirm_local_claim: This station is factory-reset, and I accept that the official app will no longer control it

progress.pairing: Pairing with the device over Bluetooth… This takes about 20 seconds.
progress.provisioning_wifi: Sending credentials to the device over Bluetooth… This takes about 15 seconds.

error.already_configured_address: Another OUPES Mega entry already uses that Bluetooth address.
error.cloud_identity_login_failed: Sign-in to the Cleanergy cloud failed. Check the email and password, or go back and choose a different method. Credentials are used once and never stored.
error.cloud_identity_no_open_id: Signed in and found the station, but the vendor's records for it did not include the numeric user ID that the Bluetooth key is derived from. The Home Assistant log names the fields that were present, so you can tell an account without one from a vendor that renamed the field. If you know the number, type it in above; if not, switch back and enter a device key you already have.
error.cloud_identity_no_user_id: Signed in and found the station, but the numeric account id (userId) could not be read from the response. Try again; if it keeps happening, enter openId and userId yourself instead.
error.cloud_identity_not_bound: This station is not in that account's device list. Add it in the Cleanergy app first — a Guardian / D5 V2 only carries the account identity after the app has bound it — then try again.
error.cloud_login_failed: Cloud login failed. Check the email and password, and make sure this is the account the station was added to. You can also go back and try a different method.
error.confirm_required: Tick the box to confirm the station is factory-reset.
error.invalid_address: Invalid Bluetooth MAC address format. Use XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX.
error.invalid_device_key: Device key must be exactly 10 hexadecimal characters (e.g. bd236b1695).
error.invalid_open_id: openId must be at most 32 characters - it is written into a fixed-size field of the authentication packet.
error.invalid_user_id: That is not a usable user ID. It is the numeric id of the Cleanergy account the station was paired with, and it is not shown anywhere in the Cleanergy app. An existing entry in Home Assistant reports it - open the cog on the OUPES card, then Configure - and a vendor password login returns it as `uid`.
error.pairing_connection_failed: Could not connect to the device. Make sure no other app (e.g. Cleanergy) is connected and the device is in pairing mode.
error.pairing_device_not_found: Device not found via Bluetooth. Make sure the device is powered on, in range, and in pairing mode (hold IoT button 5 seconds until rapid flash).
error.pairing_timeout: Pairing did not complete. Try again — make sure the device is in pairing mode (hold IoT button 5 seconds until rapid flash). The device may need a moment after the reset before it accepts pairing.
error.wifi_unsupported_guardian: Guardian / D5 V2 stations cannot be handed WiFi credentials over Bluetooth. The frame that carries your account identity and the frame that carries a network name are two different packets, and the station only accepts the identity one - so filling this in is what breaks the pairing. Leave it blank: Home Assistant talks Bluetooth, and the station does not need WiFi to work. If this appeared while reconfiguring, clear the network fields or tick *Re-run BLE pairing*.
